title: Floyd-Warshall algorithm: all-pairs shortest paths in Python — cv.cm
description: Floyd-Warshall explained: all-pairs shortest paths with three nested loops, a traced example, Python code, path reconstruction, negative cycles and O(V³) cost.
h1: Floyd-Warshall algorithm explained: how it works, code and complexity
answer: The Floyd-Warshall algorithm computes the shortest path between every pair of nodes in a weighted graph. It keeps a V × V distance matrix and, for each node k in turn, checks whether going through k makes the path from i to j shorter: `dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j])`. It handles negative edge weights, detects negative cycles, and runs in O(V³) time with O(V²) memory.

body: Sometimes you need the distance between all pairs of places, not just from one start: a table of travel times between all cities, the latency between every pair of servers, or the full reachability of a dependency graph. Floyd-Warshall solves this all-pairs shortest path problem with a very short dynamic programming algorithm.
It was published by Robert Floyd in 1962 ("Algorithm 97: Shortest path"), building on Stephen Warshall's 1962 algorithm for transitive closure.

Number the nodes 0 to V − 1. After processing node k, `dist[i][j]` is the shortest path from i to j that uses only nodes 0 to k as intermediate stops. Allowing one more intermediate node k gives two options: the old best path that avoids k, or a path i → k → j made of two best paths that already only use nodes before k.

ol: Fill the matrix: 0 on the diagonal, the edge weight where an edge exists, infinity elsewhere.
For k = 0 to V − 1, for every pair (i, j): if `dist[i][k] + dist[k][j] < dist[i][j]`, update it.
After the last k, the matrix holds all shortest distances. A negative value on the diagonal means a negative cycle.

body: The order of the loops is essential: k must be the outer loop.
Directed graph with 4 nodes and edges 0→1 (3), 0→3 (7), 1→0 (8), 1→2 (2), 2→0 (5), 2→3 (1), 3→0 (2). Start matrix (row = from, column = to):

ol: k = 0: paths may pass through node 0. 1→3 becomes 8 + 7 = 15, 2→1 becomes 5 + 3 = 8 and 3→1 becomes 2 + 3 = 5.
k = 1: through node 1. 0→2 becomes 3 + 2 = 5 and 3→2 becomes 5 + 2 = 7.
k = 2: through node 2. 0→3 improves from 7 to 5 + 1 = 6, 1→3 from 15 to 2 + 1 = 3, and 1→0 from 8 to 2 + 5 = 7.
k = 3: through node 3. 1→0 improves from 7 to 3 + 2 = 5, 2→0 from 5 to 1 + 2 = 3, and 2→1 from 8 to 1 + 5 = 6.

If you have many nodes and want speed in Python, the same triple loop can be written with NumPy as one vectorized update per k: `d = np.minimum(d, d[:, k, None] + d[None, k, :])`.

body: For sparse graphs with non-negative weights, running Dijkstra from every node costs O(V × (V + E) log V), which is faster than O(V³) when E is much smaller than V².

body.note: Putting k in the inner loop is the most common bug. The algorithm is only correct when k is the outermost loop, because each round must finish using intermediate nodes 0 to k − 1 before node k is allowed.

ul: Negative cycles: after the loops, if `dist[i][i] < 0` for some i, node i lies on a negative cycle and shortest paths through it are undefined.
Transitive closure (Warshall): use booleans and replace min/plus with or/and: `reach[i][j] = reach[i][j] or (reach[i][k] and reach[k][j])`.
Minimax and maximin paths: replace `+` with `max` (or `min`) to find, for example, the path whose largest edge is as small as possible.
Use a large finite number instead of infinity only if you are sure that the sum of two of them cannot overflow; in Python, `float("inf")` is the safe choice.
Initialize the diagonal to 0, and when there are parallel edges keep the smallest weight.

ul: Precomputing a distance table between all stations, warehouses or cities for later lookups.
Graph analytics such as closeness centrality or the diameter of a small network.
Interview problems: find the city with the smallest number of neighbors within a distance threshold, evaluate division (ratios as path products), course prerequisites as transitive closure.

faq.q: Can Floyd-Warshall handle negative edge weights?
faq.a: Yes, as long as there is no negative cycle. If there is one, some diagonal entry `dist[i][i]` becomes negative, which is how you detect it.

faq.q: Why must k be the outer loop?
faq.a: The algorithm builds solutions in stages: stage k allows only nodes 0 to k as intermediate stops. Every pair must be updated for stage k before any path is allowed to use node k + 1.

Yes. The state is the shortest path from i to j using intermediate nodes up to k, and each stage is computed from the previous one. The k dimension is dropped because updating in place does not change the result.
Use Dijkstra for one source or for large sparse graphs with non-negative weights. Use Floyd-Warshall when you need all pairs on a small or dense graph, or when there are negative weights.
